questions.stem: Under the bakuhan system of Tokugawa Japan, political power was divided between:
options: the Emperor in Kyoto and an elected council of samurai and merchants
the shogun and a Diet of nobles that met each year in Kyoto to make laws
the Buddhist temples and the merchant guilds of Osaka and Nagasaki
the shogun's government in Edo and daimyo who ruled their own domains
questions.explanation: The bakufu (the shogun's government) controlled foreign policy and the major cities, while the daimyo governed their own domains (han) under its supervision. The Emperor in Kyoto had great prestige but no real power. Japan had no elected body before 1890.

questions.stem: The Tokugawa system of sankin-kotai (alternate attendance) required daimyo to:
options: pay a yearly tribute in rice to the Emperor's court in Kyoto
send their eldest sons to study Dutch learning at Nagasaki
hand over half of every harvest to the shogun's granaries in Osaka
spend alternate years in Edo and leave their families there when away
questions.explanation: Daimyo travelled between their domains and Edo with large retinues, and their wives and heirs stayed in Edo as hostages. The cost of the journeys and two households drained the daimyo's wealth, which helped keep them from challenging the shogun.

questions.stem: Under the Tokugawa policy later known as sakoku, which foreign contact was still allowed?
options: Open trade with any Western nation at the ports of Edo and Osaka
Trade with Britain and the USA through a single port at Shimoda
Overseas voyages by Japanese merchants licensed by the shogun
Limited trade with Dutch and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki
questions.explanation: From the 1630s Christianity was banned, the Portuguese were expelled and Japanese were forbidden to travel abroad. The Dutch were confined to the island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour, and Chinese traders also used Nagasaki. Shimoda was opened only by the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854.

questions.stem: By the early 19th century many samurai were in debt. The main reason was that:
options: the shogun had confiscated both their swords and their land in the 1790s
foreign traders had flooded Japan with cheap imported rice and cloth
they were heavily taxed to pay for wars against China and Korea
their fixed rice stipends fell behind costs while merchants grew rich
questions.explanation: Samurai were paid fixed stipends in rice, but Japan's economy was becoming commercial and money-based. Merchants, officially the lowest class, lent to samurai and daimyo and grew wealthy. Japan fought no foreign wars in this period and had very little foreign trade.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Tokugawa order was already weakening before Perry arrived in 1853. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: The building of Edo Castle and the start of the sankin-kotai system
The division of society into samurai, peasants, artisans and merchants
Famines and peasant uprisings in the 1830s, and samurai deeply in debt to merchants
The ban on Christianity and the expulsion of Portuguese traders in the 1630s
questions.explanation: The Tenpo famine of the 1830s brought widespread unrest, including Oshio Heihachiro's rising in Osaka in 1837, and the indebtedness of samurai showed the class order no longer matched economic reality. The other options describe the system being set up and enforced, which are signs of strength rather than decline.

questions.stem: Commodore Matthew Perry of the US Navy first sailed into Edo Bay with his 'Black Ships' in which year?
questions.explanation: Perry arrived in July 1853 with a letter from President Fillmore and returned in early 1854 to sign the Treaty of Kanagawa. 1868 is the year of the Restoration and 1889 the year of the Meiji Constitution.

questions.stem: What did the US government mainly want from Japan when it sent Perry?
options: Ports for coal and supplies, safe treatment of shipwrecked sailors, and trade
Japanese territory for a naval base and the right to settle American colonists there
Japan's help in a war against Britain for control of the Pacific Ocean
An alliance against Russia and the right to send Christian missionaries
questions.explanation: American steamships crossing the Pacific to China and whaling ships in the north Pacific needed coaling stations and protection for shipwrecked crews, and American merchants wanted to open trade. The USA did not seek colonies in Japan or an alliance.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Kanagawa, signed with the USA in 1854:
options: ended the shogunate and restored power to the Emperor in Kyoto
opened Shimoda and Hakodate to US ships and allowed a US consul
opened every Japanese port to US merchants with no customs duties at all
gave the USA control of Edo Bay and the island of Hokkaido
questions.explanation: Kanagawa opened two remote ports for supplies, promised care for shipwrecked sailors and allowed a consul at Shimoda, where Townsend Harris arrived in 1856. Full commercial rights came only with the treaty of 1858.

questions.stem: The 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce, negotiated by Townsend Harris, is called an 'unequal treaty' mainly because it:
options: allowed the USA to station troops in Edo and to appoint Japanese officials
required Japan to buy all of its warships and weapons from the USA
gave foreigners extraterritoriality and fixed Japan's import tariffs low
forced Japan to pay the USA an indemnity for firing on its warships
questions.explanation: Americans accused of crimes in Japan were tried by their own consuls, and Japan could not change its tariffs without the treaty powers' consent. Similar treaties followed with the Netherlands, Russia, Britain and France. Removing these terms became a central aim of Meiji governments.

questions.stem: In 1858 the shogun's chief minister, Ii Naosuke, signed the commercial treaties without the Emperor's approval. Why did this weaken the shogunate?
options: It gave the daimyo of Satsuma and Choshu the right to make their own foreign treaties
The Emperor dismissed the shogun and appointed Ii Naosuke to rule in his place
Critics could rally around the Emperor against a shogunate that seemed to yield to foreigners
The Dutch ended their trade at Nagasaki, removing the shogunate's main source of foreign revenue
questions.explanation: Emperor Komei opposed the treaties, so signing them made the bakufu look both weak before the West and disloyal to the throne. Opponents took up the cause of the Emperor, and Ii was assassinated outside Edo Castle in 1860. The shogun was not dismissed by the Emperor.

questions.stem: The slogan 'sonno joi', used by opponents of the shogunate in the 1850s and 1860s, meant:
options: civilisation and enlightenment
Eastern ethics, Western science
revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians
rich country, strong army
questions.explanation: Sonno joi combined loyalty to the Emperor with hostility to the foreigners admitted by the treaties. 'Rich country, strong army' (fukoku kyohei) and 'civilisation and enlightenment' (bunmei kaika) were slogans of the Meiji government after 1868.

questions.stem: In 1863-1864 Western warships bombarded Kagoshima in Satsuma and the forts at Shimonoseki in Choshu. What was the most important effect on these two domains?
options: Their leaders gave up on expelling foreigners and turned to Western arms and methods
They signed separate treaties that placed their domains under direct British protection
They closed their ports to every foreign ship and banned all trade with the West
They lost their lands to the shogun, who used the crisis to abolish both domains
questions.explanation: Defeat showed that expulsion was impossible, so Satsuma and Choshu began buying Western weapons, building modern forces and even sending students abroad. Their new strength let them lead the overthrow of the shogunate a few years later.

questions.stem: In 1866 a secret alliance brokered by Sakamoto Ryoma of Tosa united the two domains that went on to lead the overthrow of the shogunate. They were:
options: Aizu and Kuwana
Mito and Owari
Hakodate and Nagasaki
Satsuma and Choshu
questions.explanation: The Satsuma-Choshu alliance joined former rivals against the bakufu. Aizu and Kuwana were among the shogun's most loyal supporters in the Boshin War, and Mito and Owari were branch houses of the Tokugawa family. Hakodate and Nagasaki were ports, not domains.

questions.stem: When imperial rule was restored in January 1868, the Emperor in whose name it was proclaimed was:
options: a former shogun who had been adopted into the imperial family
an adult ruler, educated in Europe, who planned the reforms himself
Emperor Komei, who had approved the Harris Treaty in 1858
the teenage Mutsuhito, who had come to the throne in 1867
questions.explanation: Mutsuhito, born in 1852, succeeded his father Komei early in 1867, and his reign name was Meiji ('enlightened rule'). Real decisions were made by a small group of oligarchs acting in his name. Komei had opposed the treaties and died in 1867.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Boshin War of 1868-1869 is accurate?
options: Forces of the new imperial government defeated supporters of the Tokugawa
Japan fought Britain and France, who sent troops to keep the shogun in power
Satsuma rebels led by Saigo Takamori were crushed by a conscript army
Peasant armies overthrew both the shogun and the daimyo in a revolution
questions.explanation: Armies led by Satsuma and Choshu defeated the former shogun's supporters, with the last resistance ending at Hakodate in 1869. The defeat of Saigo's Satsuma rebels by a conscript army was the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.

questions.stem: The Charter Oath issued in the Emperor's name in April 1868 promised that:
options: the samurai would keep their privileges and the daimyo their lands
knowledge would be sought throughout the world to strengthen imperial rule
an elected national parliament would be created with power over the Emperor
foreigners would be expelled and Japan's ports closed once more
questions.explanation: The Oath's five articles also promised deliberative assemblies, the unity of all classes, freedom for common people to pursue their callings and the abandonment of 'evil customs' of the past. It signalled that the new government would modernise rather than expel the West.

questions.stem: In 1871 the Meiji government abolished the domains (han) and replaced them with prefectures. Its main purpose was to:
options: centralise power by replacing the daimyo with governors appointed from Tokyo
reward the daimyo of Satsuma and Choshu with larger territories to rule
allow the people of each prefecture to elect their own assembly and governor
unite the domain armies in preparation for an invasion of Korea
questions.explanation: The daimyo had returned their domain registers to the Emperor in 1869; in 1871 the domains themselves were abolished. Former daimyo received pensions and the government took on their debts, which made the change easier to accept. Governors were appointed, not elected.

questions.stem: The Conscription Law of 1873 was a blow to the samurai mainly because it:
options: abolished the army and replaced it with a police force of commoners
barred former samurai from becoming officers in the new army
ended their monopoly on military service by drafting men of all classes
required every adult samurai to serve ten years in the navy without any pay
questions.explanation: Under the law, associated with Yamagata Aritomo, young men of all classes could be called up for three years. Bearing arms was no longer the hereditary privilege of the samurai, although many former samurai became officers.

questions.stem: The land tax reform of 1873 changed Japanese taxation by:
options: letting the daimyo collect taxes in rice and keep half for themselves
taxing foreign trade only, so that farm land was left untaxed
replacing rice dues with a fixed money tax on the assessed value of land
abolishing all taxes on peasants and taxing the merchants and samurai instead
questions.explanation: The tax was set at 3 per cent of the land's assessed value, payable in money by the landowner, which gave the government a stable income whatever the harvest. Peasant protests led to a cut to 2.5 per cent in 1877. The daimyo no longer existed as rulers by then.

questions.stem: The Iwakura Mission of 1871-1873 travelled to the USA and Europe in order to:
options: buy warships and recruit Western officers to command Japan's army
persuade Western governments to accept Japan's claim to Korea
seek revision of the treaties and study Western institutions and industry
sign alliances with Britain and France against Russia and China
questions.explanation: Led by Iwakura Tomomi with Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and Ito Hirobumi, the mission failed to revise the treaties but studied government, education and industry. Its members returned convinced that Japan must build its strength at home.

questions.stem: In 1873 leaders returning from the Iwakura Mission, including Okubo Toshimichi, blocked Saigo Takamori's plan to send a mission to Korea that could lead to war. What was their main reason?
options: They feared that the Emperor himself intended to lead the army into Korea
Japan needed to strengthen itself at home before it risked a foreign war
They believed Korea was already under the protection of the British Empire
They held that war with Korea would break the Charter Oath's promise of peace
questions.explanation: Having seen Western power at first hand, Okubo and his allies argued that reform, finance and industry had to come first. Saigo and other leaders resigned over the decision, and discontented samurai later rallied to him in Satsuma.

questions.stem: The Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 is significant mainly because:
options: it led directly to the abolition of the domains and the new prefectures
the government's conscript army defeated the last major samurai revolt
it forced the government to restore samurai stipends and sword rights
it was the final battle between the shogun's forces and the Emperor's
questions.explanation: Saigo Takamori led former samurai, angered by the 1876 ban on swords and the conversion of their stipends into bonds, against the government he had helped create, and died when the rising was crushed. The victory of an army of conscripted commoners showed the new state's strength. The domains had been abolished in 1871.

questions.stem: Which group provided most of the leaders of the early Meiji government?
options: Osaka merchants who had financed the overthrow of the Tokugawa
The great daimyo families who had ruled the largest domains under the shogun
Samurai from Satsuma and Choshu who had led the movement against the shogun
Court nobles in Kyoto who had controlled the Emperor for centuries
questions.explanation: Men such as Okubo, Saigo and Kido, and later Ito Hirobumi and Yamagata Aritomo, were mostly lower or middle-ranking samurai from Satsuma and Choshu, with allies from Tosa and Hizen. Some court nobles, such as Iwakura Tomomi, also held high office, but the samurai reformers dominated.

questions.stem: Fukuzawa Yukichi contributed to Meiji Japan mainly as:
options: the Satsuma leader who led the rebellion of 1877 against the state
the official who drafted the constitution after studying in Prussia
a writer and educator who promoted Western learning and independence
a general who led the imperial army in the Boshin War and later in Korea
questions.explanation: Fukuzawa founded the school that became Keio University and wrote widely read works such as An Encouragement of Learning, urging Japanese to study Western knowledge and develop personal independence. The constitution was drafted under Ito Hirobumi.

questions.stem: A key reason the Meiji government adopted Western-style legal codes and courts in the 1880s and 1890s was to:
options: let Japanese courts try cases inside Western countries
meet a condition for joining the League of Nations
satisfy samurai demands for a return to traditional law
persuade the Western powers to give up extraterritoriality
questions.explanation: The treaty powers justified extraterritoriality by claiming Japan's law was not 'civilised', so modern codes removed their excuse. The League of Nations did not exist until 1920.

questions.stem: In 1894 Japan signed the first treaty in which a Western power agreed to give up extraterritoriality, which ended in 1899. Which power signed it?
options: Britain
the USA
France
Russia
questions.explanation: The Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of July 1894 was followed by similar treaties with the other powers. Japan regained full control of its tariffs in 1911, completing the revision of the unequal treaties.

questions.stem: Ito Hirobumi modelled the Meiji Constitution of 1889 mainly on:
options: the British system, in which cabinets answer to the Commons
the US Constitution, with an elected president and separate powers
the French Republic, whose parliament chose the president
the German system, which kept strong powers for the monarch
questions.explanation: Ito studied constitutions in Europe in 1882-1883 and favoured the Prussian and German model, which preserved the monarch's authority over an elected assembly. When the cabinet system was created in 1885, Ito became Japan's first prime minister.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Meiji Constitution of 1889 most limited democracy in Japan?
options: The Diet had two houses, one of them elected by male voters
Subjects were granted rights such as free speech within the limits of law
The budget needed the approval of the elected House of Representatives
Sovereignty lay with the Emperor, and ministers were responsible to him
questions.explanation: The Emperor was declared 'sacred and inviolable' and held supreme command and the power to appoint ministers, who answered to him rather than to the Diet. The other options are features that gave the elected house and the people some role, even if limited.

questions.stem: In Japan's first general election in 1890, the right to vote was limited to:
options: all men aged 20 or over who had completed their military service
former samurai and nobles, whatever their wealth or income
men and women who could read and who owned land in their prefecture
men aged 25 or over who paid at least 15 yen a year in direct tax
questions.explanation: The tax qualification meant only about 1 per cent of the population could vote, mostly landowners. The upper house, the House of Peers, was made up of nobles and imperial appointees. Universal male suffrage came only in 1925.

questions.stem: The Imperial Rescript on Education of 1890, read aloud in schools across Japan, told students to value:
options: science and technology ahead of moral and religious instruction
loyalty to the Emperor and filial piety, serving the state in an emergency
individual freedom and critical thinking as taught in American and European schools
Buddhist teachings on peace and withdrawal from worldly affairs
questions.explanation: The Rescript combined Confucian virtues with devotion to the Emperor and the nation, and schools treated it with ceremony alongside the Emperor's portrait. It shows the government using modern mass education to build loyalty, not liberal individualism.

questions.stem: How did the Meiji government help create the large business groups later called zaibatsu?
options: It sold state-built mines and factories cheaply to private firms in the 1880s
It nationalised all private businesses and handed them over to the former daimyo
It banned foreign firms so that samurai families could run all industry
It forced the old merchant houses to merge into one national company
questions.explanation: The government built model enterprises such as the Tomioka silk mill and railways, but under Finance Minister Matsukata Masayoshi in the 1880s it sold many of them to well-connected firms. Houses such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi grew into conglomerates with close ties to the state.

questions.stem: The First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895 was fought mainly over:
options: Russia's lease of Port Arthur in southern Manchuria
foreign trading rights in Shanghai and Canton
rival Japanese and Chinese influence in Korea
control of the ports of Taiwan and the Pescadores
questions.explanation: When the Donghak rebellion broke out in Korea in 1894, both China and Japan sent troops, and war followed. Taiwan was a prize of the peace, not the cause of the war, and Russia leased Port Arthur only in 1898.

questions.stem: Under the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895), China agreed to:
options: give Japan southern Sakhalin and the railway in southern Manchuria
transfer Germany's leased territory at Qingdao in Shandong to Japan
recognise Korea's independence and cede Taiwan, the Pescadores and Liaodong
hand Korea over to Japan as a colony and pay no indemnity of any kind
questions.explanation: China also paid a large indemnity and opened more ports to trade. Southern Sakhalin and the South Manchurian Railway came from Russia in 1905, and Qingdao was seized from Germany in 1914.

questions.stem: Why did the Triple Intervention of 1895 cause such anger in Japan?
options: Russia, Britain and Germany demanded a share of the indemnity Japan had won from China
The Western powers refused to recognise Korean independence and kept Korea under Chinese rule
Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to give up the Liaodong Peninsula, which Russia then leased
Britain, the USA and France forced Japan to hand Taiwan back to China within a year of the war
questions.explanation: Japan had to return the Liaodong Peninsula in exchange for extra payment, and Russia leased its tip, including Port Arthur, in 1898. The episode convinced many Japanese that only greater military power would earn respect, and it fed rivalry with Russia.

questions.stem: Japan's 1876 Treaty of Ganghwa with Korea opened Korean ports and gave Japanese in Korea extraterritorial rights. What does this best show about Meiji Japan?
options: Japan wanted Korea as an equal ally to resist the Western powers together
Korea had asked Japan for protection against Chinese control of its government
Japan was carrying out a demand from Britain that Korea open itself to trade
Japan was imposing on a neighbour the kind of unequal treaty the West had imposed on it
questions.explanation: Japan used gunboat diplomacy against Korea much as Perry had used it against Japan, and the treaty's terms copied the unequal treaties. It shows Japan learning the methods of Western imperialism while still seeking to escape them itself.

questions.stem: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902 was important to Japan mainly because it:
options: ended Japan's isolation and kept other powers out of a war with Russia
committed Britain to fight beside Japan in any war against Russia
handed Japan the British naval base at Hong Kong for twenty years
gave Japan a permanent seat on a council of the great powers
questions.explanation: Each ally would stay neutral if the other fought one power, and would help if a second power joined in. This meant Japan could fight Russia in 1904 without fear that France or Germany would intervene as in 1895. It was the first alliance on equal terms between Japan and a Western power.

questions.stem: Japan opened the Russo-Japanese War in February 1904 with:
options: an invasion of the Russian port of Vladivostok
the naval battle in the Tsushima Strait
the occupation of Beijing by Japanese troops
a surprise attack on the Russian fleet at Port Arthur
questions.explanation: Japanese torpedo boats attacked the Russian squadron at Port Arthur, and the port fell after a long siege. The Battle of Tsushima in May 1905, in which Russia's Baltic fleet was destroyed, came near the end of the war.

questions.stem: Historians debate whether the events of 1868 were a 'restoration' or a 'revolution'. Which evidence best supports calling them a revolution?
options: The Emperor's authority was justified by appeals to ancient Shinto tradition
Within a decade the domains, the samurai class and the old class order had been abolished
Power was returned in name to the Emperor, whose line was claimed to stretch back centuries
The new leaders came mainly from the samurai class of the Tokugawa order
questions.explanation: The speed and scale of change to Japan's political, social and economic structure supports the case for a revolution. The return of power to the throne and the appeal to ancient tradition support the label 'restoration', and the samurai origins of the leaders suggest continuity.

questions.stem: Historians who describe the Meiji Restoration as a 'revolution from above' mean that:
options: a small elite transformed Japan through state power, not a popular rising
the Emperor personally planned and directed every one of the reforms
peasants and workers seized power and then chose new leaders to govern
Western powers imposed the new system after defeating the shogun's army
questions.explanation: The phrase stresses that the changes were driven by oligarchs using the state, while peasants and townspeople had little say. E. H. Norman's Japan's Emergence as a Modern State (1940) argued that this left authoritarian features that later helped militarism grow.

questions.stem: From the 1960s some Western historians presented Meiji Japan as a model of successful modernisation. Critics of this view most often point to:
options: Japan's defeats in its wars against China in 1895 and Russia in 1905
authoritarian rule, heavy burdens on the countryside and a path to militarism
Japan's failure to build any modern industry or railways before 1912
the survival of the shogun as the real ruler behind the Emperor
questions.explanation: Modernisation theorists stressed rapid industrialisation, education and stable government. Critics, including Marxist historians, emphasised the limited franchise, repression, peasant poverty and the link between Meiji institutions and later aggression. Japan won both wars and built extensive industry and railways.
